assumptions: source assumption: uniform circular motion at constant angular speed, so one revolution (2π radians) takes exactly one period T (Tatum Fig. VIII.3 derivation context).

limitations: Uniform (mean) motion only; osculating angular speed on eccentric orbits varies within a revolution and needs the vis-viva treatment (deferred).

assumptions: source assumption: near-surface free fall where the separation of centers equals the body radius (r = R_E, Fig. 13.7) and the falling mass m cancels, so surface gravity depends only on the body (Eq. 13.2).

application profile: g is the measured free-fall acceleration at the surface and R the volumetric-mean-equivalent spherical radius; rotation/apparent-weight corrections are excluded (see limitations).

gaps: Requires vocabulary extension: new meanings surface_gravity and body_radius (or reuse once defined). Shares central_mass with the dynamical records: gravimetric (g·R²/G) and orbital (4π²a³/G·T²) mass determinations are complementary, not duplicates.

models.inverse_notes: Surface gravity solves as g = 6.67e-11*M/R**2 (Eq. 13.2 itself); substitution check with the text values (M = 5.96e24 kg, R = 6.37e6 m) returns g = 9.797 m/s² against 9.80 m/s². limitations: Spherical, non-rotating idealization: the text notes g varies equator-to-pole (~0.5%) and apparent weight differs under rotation (§13.2); high-precision geodesy needs those corrections, not this record.
Scoped to the surface radius; the identical altitude form (text's 8.67 m/s² ISS-altitude example) is a different stated context and is not claimed here.
Requires an independently measured G (Cavendish tradition); before G, no absolute masses were knowable (source significance note).

assumptions: source assumption: Newtonian two-body mutual revolution about the common center of mass (the §18.5 seesaw passage); both masses enter symmetrically through their sum, with no negligible-mass approximation.

derived transcription: the §18.2 solar-unit law D³ = (M1+M2)·P² is combined with the §13.4 SI derivation (T = 2π√(r³/GM) squaring to T² = 4π²a³/GM) to give the SI mass-sum form; both parent statements are source-backed and the combination is shown in the translation notes.
application profile: a is the relative-orbit semi-major axis (orbit of one body with respect to the other, per §18.2); component masses supplied for the stated system and epoch.

gaps: Requires vocabulary extension: new meanings binary_component_mass (×2 roles distinguished by context, or reuse central_mass/orbiting_mass with a binary context) and reuse of orbital_period_squared/semi_major_axis; new unit s^2. No operator extension needed.

models.inverse_notes: Mass sum solves as M1+M2 = 39.47841760435743*a**3/(6.67e-11*T2); substitution check with the Sirius SI numbers (a = 2.992e12 m, T2 = (1.57788e9 s)²) returns 6.365e30 kg = 3.20 solar masses against the worked 3.2. Individual masses are not separately determined by this record (velocities plus orientation needed, per §18.2). Requires T2 > 0 beyond the declared output domain. Do not publish rearrangements as separate records.
limitations: Two-body mutual revolution only; triple/quadruple hierarchies (Mizar) and perturbed systems excluded.
Yields only the mass sum; individual masses need relative velocities and orbit orientation (§18.2) — a different determination, not claimed here.
Ideal Newtonian dynamics; relativistic corrections excluded.

references.method: Published Sirius worked example (§18.2): separation about 20 AU (= 2.992e12 m via Appendix D 1.496e11 m/AU) and period about 50 yr (= 1.57788e9 s via 365.25 d), mass sum 3.2 solar masses split here as 2.0 + 1.2 (any split summing to 3.2 exercises the sum; component split is not asserted). Expected is the 50 yr period squared. Tolerance 2e17 (8%) bounds the 'about' qualifier on 20 AU (cubically amplified) and 50 yr.
references.provenance: Published worked result converted to SI with documented scales; tests the mass-sum transcription, not arithmetic replay.

models.summary: Gravitational potential energy of a mass pair with the zero-at-infinity convention.
models.title: Gravitational potential energy of a pair

variables.context: Same mass pair and epoch as M, m and r.
variables.definition: Gravitational potential energy of the pair (zero at infinite separation; negative when bound).
variables.domain: Non-positive finite energy in J (zero only at the m = 0 boundary or infinite separation).

variables.context: Same mass pair and epoch as U, m and r.
variables.definition: Mass of the dominant body of the pair.
variables.source_symbol: M_E generalized to M (source uses M_E, M generally)

variables.context: Same mass pair and epoch as U, M and r.
variables.definition: Mass of the second body of the pair.
variables.domain: Nonnegative finite mass in kg; zero admits the no-pair boundary (U = 0).

variables.context: Same mass pair and epoch as U, M and m.
variables.definition: Center-to-center separation of the pair.
variables.source_symbol: r (source uses r1, r2 for separations; r for the pair distance)

assumptions: source assumption: Newtonian circular orbit where gravity supplies the centripetal force; the kinetic term K = ½·m·v² with the circular speed of Eq. 13.7 gives K = G·m·M/(2r) (§13.4 derivation).
Orbiter mass m and central mass M supplied for the stated system and epoch.

gaps: Requires vocabulary extension: new meaning circular_orbit_kinetic_energy (or reuse once defined), new unit J for this port. No operator extension needed.
Completes the circular-orbit energy triple with the potential (U = −GmM/r) and total (E = −GmM/2r) records: K = −E = −U/2, three independently meaningful quantities sharing one section's derivation.

models.inverse_notes: Orbiter mass solves as m = 2*K*r/(6.67e-11*M); substitution check with the ½·m·v²-route ISS value (K = 2.6473005e11 J, r = 6.77e6 m, M = 5.96e24 kg) returns m = 9016.6 kg against 9000 kg (0.2%, within oracle rounding). Radius and central-mass inversions combine K with the speed law and are not separately published. The m = 0 boundary gives K = 0 (no moving mass, no kinetic energy).
limitations: Uniform circular motion only; varying speed on eccentric orbits needs the vis-viva treatment (deferred).
Non-relativistic kinetic energy (½·m·v²); speeds approaching c need relativity, excluded here.
Ideal two-body motion only; thrust, drag and perturbations excluded.

references.method: Independent route through the kinetic definition: K = ½·m·v² with the published ISS speed 7.67e3 m/s (Soyuz mass 9000 kg), giving 2.6473005e11 J. Tolerance 1e9 (0.38%) covers 3-significant-figure print rounding.
references.provenance: Published speed combined with the elementary kinetic definition — independent of the G·M/r substitution under test.

references.method: Independent route: K = ½·m·v² with NASA's mean orbital velocity 29.78 km/s, giving 2.647242474e33 J. Tolerance 1e31 covers near-circular deviation and rounding.
references.provenance: Independent agency velocity combined with the kinetic definition.

rejection_cases.reason: Zero radius is not an orbit (division by zero); guard r > 0 rejects it.
Orbiter mass scales the kinetic energy and cannot be assumed.

relationship.locator: §13.4 'Energy in Circular Orbits': 'the right side is just twice the kinetic energy, so we have K = ½·m·v² = G·m·M_E/(2r)'.
relationship.translation_notes: Verbatim transcription of the stated kinetic-energy form. G inlined as the printed literal with constants metadata; the integer 2 is exact from the ½ kinetic factor (pure arithmetic literal, documented here). No conversion inlined — coherent in base SI units. Dimensional check: (L³/(M·T²))·M·M/L = M·L²/T² (energy). r2 mechanical revision (review-directed, no science change): the bare G literal is replaced by the runtime registry name gravitational_constant (CODATA 2022 value 6.67430e-11 m3/(kg*s2)), resolved by runtime 0.23.0+ through the registry scales; no conversion factor is inlined and the inlined-literal constants entry is removed.

sources.evidence: Multiplies Newton's law by r to show the right side is twice the kinetic energy, giving K = ½·m·v² = G·m·M_E/(2r), then sums with U for Eq. 13.9.

models.summary: Kinetic energy of a circular orbiter from both masses and the orbit radius.
models.title: Circular-orbit kinetic energy from masses and radius

variables.context: Same two-body system and epoch as m, M and r.
variables.definition: Kinetic energy of the orbiter on its uniform circular orbit.
variables.domain: Nonnegative finite energy in J (zero only at the m = 0 boundary).

variables.context: Same two-body system and epoch as K, M and r.
variables.definition: Mass of the negligible-mass orbiter whose kinetic energy is evaluated.
variables.domain: Nonnegative finite mass in kg; zero admits the no-orbiter boundary (K = 0).

variables.context: Same two-body system and epoch as K, m and r; stated body, never assumed.
variables.definition: Mass of the central body that dominates the two-body dynamics (same definition as the central-mass records).

variables.context: Same two-body system and epoch as K, m and M.
variables.definition: Circular orbit radius measured from the central-body center (same definition as the orbit-radius records).

assumptions: source assumption: Newtonian two-body conservative dynamics about the common centre of mass with total mass BOLD-M = M1+M2; the ellipse branch (E < 0) of the energy-per-unit-mass relations is used.

derived transcription: the specific-energy statement E = ½V² − G·BOLD-M/r (Eq. 9.5.30) is combined with the ellipse energy E = −G·BOLD-M/2a (Eq. 9.5.27b); both parent statements are source-printed and the one-line combination is shown here.
application profile: r is the instantaneous separation and a the relative semi-major axis for the stated pair and epoch; bound ellipses satisfy r < 2a (guard).

gaps: Requires vocabulary extension: new meaning vis_viva_velocity_squared (or reuse once defined), new unit m^2/s^2, reuse of central_mass/binary masses and lengths. No operator extension needed.

Generalizes the b01 circular record (r = a recovers V² = G·M/a per Eq. 9.5.34) and the b02 escape record (a → ∞ recovers V² = 2G·M/r per Eq. 9.5.32); kept as the distinct general law, not a duplicate.

models.inverse_notes: Semi-major axis solves as a = 1/(2/r − v2/(6.67e-11*(M1+M2))); substitution check with the Earth-perihelion oracle returns a = 1.49598e11 m exactly. Requires the bound condition v2 < 2·G·(M1+M2)/r beyond the declared domains (unbound inputs belong to the hyperbolic record, not this one). The circular (r = a) and parabolic (a → ∞) limits reproduce the b01 and b02 records and must not be re-published. Do not publish rearrangements as separate records.
limitations: Bound (elliptical) branch only: E < 0 ⟺ r < 2a, enforced by the guard; parabolic and hyperbolic branches are separate regimes (the parabolic limit is the b02 escape record).
Two-body Newtonian dynamics; perturbations, relativity and non-gravitational forces excluded.
Eccentricity does not appear: the law holds for all bound eccentricities at the stated instantaneous radius, which is its scope — not a circular restriction.

references.method: Earth perihelion radius 147.095M km (NASA Earth Fact Sheet) with semi-major axis 149.598M km against the published perihelion speed ≈ 30.3 km/s (tertiary orbital-speed tabulation, consistent with the NASA max 30.29 km/s bound). Tolerance 5e6 (0.54%) covers tertiary rounding and near-Keplerian deviation.
references.provenance: Tertiary perihelion-speed value against independent agency distance data; tests the general (r ≠ a) path no other record exercises.

references.method: Circular-consistency limit (r = a recovers Eq. 9.5.34 / b01 record): lunar numbers from §13.4 (r = 3.84e8 m, M_E = 5.96e24 kg) with Appendix D moon mass 7.36e22 kg against the published mean speed 1.022 km/s. Tolerance 1e4 (0.96%) covers the e = 0.055 circularization and print rounding.
references.provenance: Published mean speed against textbook separation and mass data; checks the r = a limit, not arithmetic replay.

rejection_cases.reason: Radius beyond twice the semi-major axis (r = 3a) is unbound for this ellipse branch (negative v²); the bound guard rejects it — hyperbolic inputs belong to the excess-speed record.
The total mass sets the energy scale; neither component may be assumed.

relationship.locator: Tatum §9.4 Eqs. 9.5.27b (E = −G·BOLD-M/2a), 9.5.30 (E = ½V² − G·BOLD-M/r) and 9.5.31 (ellipse V² = G·BOLD-M(2/r − 1/a)); negligible-mass restatement 9.5.37.
relationship.original_equation: V² = G·BOLD-M·(2/r − 1/a) for the ellipse (Eq. 9.5.31), where BOLD-M = M+m is the total mass; V² = GM(2/r − 1/a) for negligible orbiter mass (Eq. 9.5.37).
relationship.translation_notes: Direct transcription of Eq. 9.5.31 with local symbols M1, M2 (source M, m) and total mass M1+M2 (source BOLD-M). G inlined as the session printed literal with constants metadata; Tatum prints no SI G (works with GM_sun = 4π² in AU/yr units). No conversion inlined — coherent in base SI units. Dimensional check: (L³/(M·T²))·M·(1/L) = L²/T². Output name carries the square (v2). r2 mechanical revision (review-directed, no science change): the bare G literal is replaced by the runtime registry name gravitational_constant (CODATA 2022 value 6.67430e-11 m3/(kg*s2)), resolved by runtime 0.23.0+ through the registry scales; no conversion factor is inlined and the inlined-literal constants entry is removed.

sources.evidence: Derives the two-body energy integral: specific energy E = ½V² − G·BOLD-M/r (Eq. 9.5.30) combined with ellipse energy E = −G·BOLD-M/2a (Eq. 9.5.27b) to give V² = G·BOLD-M(2/r − 1/a) (Eq. 9.5.31); also prints the parabola (9.5.32), hyperbola (9.5.33), circle (9.5.34), negligible-mass (9.5.37) and GM_sun = 4π² unit-note forms.
